note: Every term a newcomer to Singapore's government would not know, and where the game introduces it. Not loaded by the game: test/jargon.js checks that each term's first appearance in a career is on one of its entry points, a card whose story makes the meaning clear. `meaning` is for writers and never appears in the game. `match` is a JavaScript regular expression for the term's uses; `skip` lists phrases it must not match. An entry point is a card id, "start" (the start screen), "header" (rank, grade and ministry), or a path into game.json or rival.json for lines shown outside cards.

terms.meaning: Currently Estimated Potential: HR's private estimate of the highest grade an officer will ever reach, set early and never told to them.
Each year senior officers rank officers of the same grade against each other; only the top of the ranking is promoted.
The yearly performance grade (A, B+, B, C, D) that decides promotion; written by your reporting officer.
Your direct boss in the service: the person who writes your appraisal.
The service's salary grades: MX13 at the bottom up to MX9, then Superscale and Staff Grade; MR4 to MR1 for ministers.
A short internal memo that sets out a problem and a recommendation, sent up the line for a decision.
A government agency set up by its own Act of Parliament, run at arm's length from its ministry (HDB, CPF Board, LTA).
A security marking for documents that may be read only by the officers they are sent to.
A high security classification; reading such a document needs clearance at that level.
The office that logs, stores and tracks every classified document in a building.
A committee of officials from several ministries set up to settle a question none can settle alone.
The officers who write a committee's papers and minutes and do its work between meetings.
The Public Service Commission: awards government scholarships, holds the bond, and appoints and disciplines senior officers.
The Public Service Division of the Prime Minister's Office: runs the civil service's careers, pay and training.
The years of service a government scholar must serve in return for the scholarship; leaving early means paying damages.
People, usually family, who sign the bond deed with a scholar and promise to pay if the scholar breaks it.
In the service, an officer who studied on a government scholarship, expected to rise fast.
The elite scheme of the civil service from which Permanent Secretaries are drawn.
The Auditor-General's Office: audits government ministries and agencies and reports to Parliament.
An official instruction or notice sent round to every officer or agency it concerns.
Dinner-and-dance: a division's annual party, with a theme, a band and a lucky draw.
The Chinese New Year custom of tossing a raw-fish salad (yusheng) high while shouting good wishes.
The Hungry Ghost month of the lunar calendar, when the spirits of the dead are said to roam.
State honours announced each National Day; the medals (pingat) are presented at an investiture.
The most senior civil servant in a ministry, answering to its Minister.
The rank just below Permanent Secretary; runs part of a ministry.
The government's job portal, where most officers apply.
The Singapore Armed Forces.
The official word-for-word record of everything said in Parliament.
The hour when MPs put questions to ministers in Parliament, filed in advance as Parliamentary Questions.
A follow-up question an MP may ask straight after a minister's answer, without notice.
Parliament, as its members call it.
The party's officer in Parliament who makes sure its MPs attend and vote as the party decides.
When the Prime Minister moves ministers and office holders between jobs.
An MP's weekly evening session where residents bring their problems and volunteers write appeal letters for them.
Group Representation Constituency: a large ward where voters elect a team of MPs together.
Single Member Constituency: a ward that elects one MP, who runs alone.
To run in an election as a candidate.

terms.meaning: The ruling party's first, informal approach to someone it may field at an election: an invitation to tea.
An MP's or candidate's walk through a market, hawker centre or estate, meeting residents.
The day candidates file their papers to stand in an election; campaigning starts then.
The day before polling day, when campaigning is banned.
An early count of a sample of votes, published on election night before the full result.
Election day, when voters cast their votes.
The weeks of Budget debate when Parliament goes through each ministry's spending and ministers announce new schemes.
Government Parliamentary Committee: the ruling party's backbenchers who shadow one ministry.
An MP who holds no office in the government.
The seats in Parliament where ministers sit; the ministers themselves.
A new MP's first speech in Parliament.
The speech that opens each term of Parliament, setting out the government's plans; MPs then debate it.
Parliament's rule book; its Standing Orders Committee decides how the rules apply.
The senior minister who leads a party's team of candidates in a GRC.
The party's local office and volunteers in an MP's ward.
The person, usually the ruling party's MP or candidate, appointed to advise a ward's community organisations.
A ward's community committees (Citizens' Consultative Committee, Residents' Committee, Community Club Management Committee), run by grassroots volunteers.
The body, run by a ward's MPs, that maintains and manages the HDB estates in it.
Extra pay for ministers and senior officials, from none up to six months' salary, tied to four national numbers.
Income at the 20th percentile: the income of a worker paid less than four in five workers; one of the National Bonus's four numbers.
The President's official residence, where ministers are sworn in.
The Prime Minister's yearly speech to the nation in August, in several languages.
Member of Parliament.
The standing partnership of the government, the unions and the employers, which sets wage guidelines together.
The law against online falsehoods: a minister can direct a post's author to attach a correction notice to it.
Central Provident Fund: the compulsory savings account every worker pays into, for retirement, housing and health.
The Housing and Development Board: builds and sells the public flats most Singaporeans live in.
Build-To-Order: a new HDB flat, sold by ballot before it is built.
An HDB flat bought second-hand from its owner, at market price.
A newer HDB town, further out and with fewer amenities; flats there are cheaper.
HDB's three classes of flat: Plus and Prime flats are more central and subsidised more, and come with longer stays and repayments when sold.
An HDB flat with three bedrooms and a living room.
Singapore's train system.
Electronic Road Pricing: road tolls charged automatically at gantries, by time of day.
The open ground floor of an HDB block, used for meeting, chess, weddings and funerals.
Coffee, local style, from a coffee shop.
An open-air food court of cheap food stalls; a hawker runs one.
Co-curricular activity: a school club or sport every student joins.
The national exam at the end of primary school, which decides secondary school places.
A government outpatient clinic in a housing estate.
The national basic health insurance scheme.
The National Parks Board: runs parks and the trees along roads.
The national water agency.
The Singapore Tourism Board.
The tax authority.
The Ministry of Finance.
The National Environment Agency.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Ministry of Health, of Transport, of Social and Family Development, of National Development.
Service and conservancy charges: the monthly fee HDB residents pay their Town Council.
A multi-storey car park in an HDB estate.
The Pan-Island Expressway.
Singapore's main English-language daily newspaper.
The Straits Times's letters page.
A Singapore online forum, famous for its long, angry threads.
How Singaporeans address or describe an older woman or man, family or not.
A market of fresh food stalls, meat, fish and vegetables.
A village, of the kind Singapore had before the HDB estates.
The statue of a lion's head on a fish's body at Marina Bay, Singapore's emblem for tourists.
